title: The Secret of the Starry Light
markdown:
Imagine the Obsidian Peaks, a place so high the air was thin and crisp, like biting into a frosty apple. Tucked among those towering mountains was the Starfall Observatory, its great silver dome a watchful eye, always gazing upwards. Night came early there. The wind made a thin music in the gantries. Commander Sol made her home in that place of starlight and quiet wonder. Her face showed a thousand nights spent looking at the stars, every line a testament to curiosity. Beside her was Rafi. Rafi was a pilot, but not just any pilot. Their hands had a special touch when they guided the observatory’s drones, making those metal birds hum with life. And then there was Thimble. A magpie with feathers like polished jet, nest a dazzling collection of trinkets. A keen eye for glitter, and a sharper mind for noticing what others missed.

One evening, as shy stars began to prickle the twilight, Commander Sol stood by the largest telescope. Her brow creased with a small worry. “Rafi. Come look at this. Something’s coming our way, and it’s moving oddly.”

Rafi hurried over, fingers already eager. On the main screen, a tiny speck, brighter than it should be, was growing. It did not act like a shooting star. It seemed too purposeful. “It’s strange. Our usual scans can’t identify it. I think we need a closer look. The Spectro-Scout is our best option.”

Sol nodded, gaze fixed. “I’ve prepped it. Sensors made to catch the faintest light, the slightest changes. Get it close enough to analyse that light. We need to know what it is, and if it’s a danger.”

Rafi’s heart gave a little jump, worry mixed with excitement. A real space mystery in the vast quiet of the sky. Thimble, perched on a railing, tilted its head, a bright glint in intelligent eyes. The object, even from this distance, had a captivating gleam. “Understood, Commander.” Rafi headed for the drone bay, already calculating paths.

The Spectro-Scout, a marvel with delicate sensor arms, was readied and launched. It soared into the inky blackness, a tiny determined spark of cleverness chasing an even tinier visitor. Rafi’s fingers flew across the console, focus absolute, guiding with an almost natural skill. The drone’s telemetry ticked. A pause, there, in the dome: heaters ticking, Thimble’s claws ticking on metal, the universe not ticking at all. Thimble, drawn by the shifting lights, fluttered to a higher perch, a silent keen-eyed observer.

As the Scout drew nearer, Sol adjusted the main telescope — not to cook the object, but to give them a clean look at the sunlight it threw back. “We’ll give the sensors something to work with. Pay close attention to the light.”

When that concentrated beam washed over the mass, something wonderful happened. The object did not merely bounce glare. Faint bands of colour, like the thinnest slivers of a rainbow, flickered across its surface. Thimble, sharp-eyed, was first. “Chirp! Shiny colours!”

Rafi, watching the incoming data, gasped. “Spectral features. Distinct lines — reds, blues, greens. A signature. These aren’t random. They match patterns I’ve studied in the lab.”

Sol’s smile widened. “That’s the curious thing about light, and about matter. Elements leave fingerprints in a spectrum — dark lines where they swallow particular colours, bright ones where they give them back. Study those fingerprints, and you can tell what something is made of, even far away.”

Rafi focused the Scout’s analysis tools. The sensors worked diligently, capturing wavelengths, the fine details of the light. Rafi compared the captured data with digital libraries, familiar patterns appearing. A moment of holding still. Then: “Mostly silicon and oxygen. Tiny bits of carbon. Not a hostile craft. A dense piece of space debris — maybe a fragment of a mineral-rich asteroid, nudged our way.”

Sol let out a long contented sigh. “Well done. And well observed, Thimble.” The magpie puffed with pride.

“So the light tells us what it’s made of?”

“Indeed. As a fingerprint identifies a person, a spectrum identifies composition. We did not have to get dangerously close.”

Thimble hopped onto Rafi’s shoulder, nudging them gently with its beak. Rafi absently scratched the bird’s head, gaze drifting upwards toward the vast expanse. The stars were no longer just distant impersonal pinpricks, but places filled with untold stories, each waiting patiently to be read. The more you looked, the more the universe seemed eager to share its secrets, one radiant silent whisper at a time. For Rafi and Thimble, curiosity thoroughly sparked, they could not wait to see what other wonders the light might yet reveal.
characters: Rafi (a drone pilot), Thimble (a magpie), Sol (a commander)
